input.question: If someone receives a full organ transplant will the organ be eventually replaced by the host's cells or will it remain as the the donor's cells for the rest of the host's life.
input.ground_truth: It will always be the donor's cells. It can be possible to wean off of antirejection drugs as your body gets used to the new organ, but if your whole liver is replaced by a donor liver, you do not have any of your own liver cells to replicate and replace the donor cells.

Okay! Imagine you have a toy car, but your toy car is broken. Your friend gives you a brand new toy car to use. You put your friend’s toy car in your toy box and play with it every day.

Now, will your toy car slowly turn into your own toy car, made by you? No! Your friend’s toy car will stay just the way it is, unless it breaks. Your body is a little like that toy box. If someone gets a new heart (or another organ) from a donor, the new heart is like your friend’s toy car. It stays the donor’s heart, not your body’s. Your body’s own cells usually don’t change the donor’s organ into your own. So, the new organ stays mostly like the donor’s for a long time. But your body does try to take care of it and sometimes, over many years, a tiny bit of change can happen, but mostly it stays the donor’s.
